nameStory: The wood lily earned its common name from its preference for growing in woodland clearings and forest edges, rather than in deep shade or open meadows. Its other nickname, 'flame lily,' comes from its brilliant orange-red petals that seem to flicker like flames when they catch the sunlight through the forest canopy.
description: Wood lily is a striking native wildflower that stands 2-4 feet tall on a single sturdy stem. It produces one to several large, upward-facing flowers that are bright orange-red with darker spots near the base of each petal. The plant has narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in whorls (circles) around the stem, giving it a distinctive layered appearance that's easy to spot even before it blooms.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large orange-red flowers face upward like cups, with six pointed petals covered in dark purple-black spots near the center. The flowers feel waxy and substantial to the touch, measuring 3-4 inches across.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in distinct whorls of 3-8 leaves per circle around the stem. The leaves feel smooth and have parallel veins running lengthwise.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single unbranched stem rising 2-4 feet tall, topped with 1-5 flowers. The plant emerges from an underground bulb and has a neat, architectural appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops upright capsules that split open to reveal flat, papery seeds stacked like coins. The dried capsules rattle when shaken and persist into fall.

habitat: Wood lilies prefer well-drained, slightly acidic soils in partial shade to full sun. In New England, look for them along woodland edges, in forest clearings, meadow borders, and sometimes in sandy or rocky areas. They're often found growing with blueberries, bracken fern, and oak or pine trees.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge in late spring, showing the characteristic whorled leaf arrangement. Plants are easily spotted by their distinctive tiered leaves even before flowering begins.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from late June through August, with peak flowering in July. The brilliant orange-red flowers are unmistakable and attract butterflies and hummingbirds.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, turning brown and splitting open. The foliage yellows and dies back, leaving the rattling seed pods visible.
seasonality.winter: Plants are completely dormant underground. Only dried stem bases and old seed capsules might remain visible above ground in protected spots.

funFact: Wood lily bulbs can live for decades and actually prefer forest fires - the bulbs survive underground while the fire clears competing vegetation and creates the perfect sunny openings these lilies love to colonize.
confusionNotes: Wood lilies are sometimes confused with tiger lilies, but tiger lilies have downward-facing flowers and small black bulbils (tiny bulbs) growing along the stem. Remember: wood lilies look UP at the sky, tiger lilies look DOWN at the ground.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'tiger lily' in some regions, this plant is completely different from the orange tiger lily commonly grown in gardens. The garden tiger lily is an Asian species with drooping flowers, while our native wood lily holds its flowers proudly upright.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives Canada lily and Turk's-cap lily which have downward-facing or nodding flowers, wood lily is the only native lily in New England that consistently faces its flowers upward. Tiger lily (the non-native garden escape) faces down and has those telltale black bulbils on the stem, while wood lily's stem is clean and smooth.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's true lilies, Canada lily is the only one with consistently downward-facing, bell-shaped flowers in yellow to orange shades.
Among New England's lilies, tiger lily is the only one with black bulbils in the leaf joints and the only non-native species commonly encountered.

Among New England's native lilies, Turk's-cap lily is the tallest and most dramatic, with its hanging orange flowers and completely recurved petals setting it apart from the upward-facing Canada lily and the smaller, red Wood lily.
Among New England's true lilies, Michigan lily is distinguished by its moderate height (shorter than Turk's-cap lily but taller than wood lily) and its orange color with backward-curved petals.
Unlike our native Canada lily and Turk's-cap lily which have drooping, downward-facing flowers, Formosa lily blooms face outward horizontally.
Unlike our native lilies, martagon lily has distinctly whorled leaves rather than alternate or scattered leaf arrangements.
